The first day

What actually happens, in order, from nothing installed to a room you can sit in.

Not how long it takes. That depends entirely on what you bring, and no honest page can tell you.

Rough prototype, thrown away afterwards. Every word here is a stand-in for hers. The pictures are real: they are from one genuinely cold first run, screen by screen, with no key.

step by step

1

what you need

A computer and a terminal — the black window where you type commands. That is the honest entry price, and it is the one thing that will stop some people. It has been tested on Macs. Nothing else has to be installed: no account, no card, no key, nothing downloaded in the background.

2

getting it

⚠️ You cannot yet. The room's own code is not public. This page describes what happens when it is, so that nobody has to guess — and so that when it opens, nothing here is a surprise. The one thing you can do today is walk around a finished room, further down.

3

you type one line

your terminal
$ python3 server.py --setup

The Study Room — setup
...

There is no installer and nothing to download. You put the room's folder somewhere, open a terminal in it, and run one command. Everything below is what it prints back.

4

it tells you the whole bargain before you decide

your terminal
The Study Room — setup

Before you paste a key

Your things stay on this computer. Nothing is uploaded, and nothing runs
unless you ask for it.

Four things are better when a big model reads them. Big models mostly live
in other people's data centres, so for these the room sends a copy of the
text to the AI service you give a key to, and reads the answer back:

    your reflection · the librarian's note · connections across the things
    you brought back · finding an older thing to show you

A reflection can go back and forth. Anything you write back is sent too,
and each time, your writing goes with it again.

Each can run on a model on your own machine instead — you'll be asked the
first time one comes up.

One thing needs a key and can't be done on your machine: changing a setting
by telling the librarian. Without a key you change settings yourself in
Manage, which always works.

Reading your photos, sorting what arrives and tidying your vault need no key
at all and never leave this computer.

Cost: reflections are nearly the whole bill, and are well under a dollar
each. Everything else rounds to nothing. Your real bill is on your
provider's own usage page — the room never guesses at it.

You can stop here and not give a key.                     more: LIBRARIAN.md

Your own machine is free. Its models are about 5 GB, and this setup does
not download them: it tells you what is missing and what to type.

Two files exist now, and they are yours to read, edit or delete:
  settings:  /Users/you/.study-room/settings.json
  keys:      /Users/you/.study-room/keys.json   (readable only by you)

anthropic — no key saved
  press Enter    leave it exactly as it is
  y              type a key now (it will not be shown)
  env            save nothing here; you will set the shell variable yourself
  choice: 
  left exactly as it is.

openai — no key saved
  press Enter    leave it exactly as it is
  y              type a key now (it will not be shown)
  env            save nothing here; you will set the shell variable yourself
  choice: 
  left exactly as it is.

Your own machine:
  running, with the language model.
  models seen:        nomic-embed-text:v1.5, qwen2.5vl:7b, qwen2.5:7b
  Nothing here is downloaded for you.

What the room has now:
  anthropic    no key
  openai       no key

Run this again any time — it is how a key is changed or removed.
To open the room:  python3 server.py

This is the real thing it prints on a machine with no key, word for word. It says what would be sent and to whom, what never leaves, that the expensive part is well under a dollar and everything else rounds to nothing — and it says you can stop here and not give a key before it asks you anything. Press Enter twice and you have a room that runs entirely on your own machine, for nothing.

5

then you start it

your terminal
$ python3 server.py

The Study Room
  library: /Users/you/StudyRoom
  serving at http://127.0.0.1:8747
  open http://127.0.0.1:8747 in your browser to begin
  press Ctrl+C when you are done

One more line and it is running — on your own machine, at an address only your computer can reach. Then you open that address.

6

and it is a room

One command starts it. It says where your library is, which address to open in your browser, and how to stop it. Then you open that address and it is a room, on your own machine, that nothing else can reach.

7

it asks who reads your writing

Before anything, it tells you who would be doing the reading, and asks. Your own machine is free. It makes two small files — your settings and your keys — and tells you where they are, so you can read them, change them, or delete them.

8

you say what to stay out of

Then it asks what it must not look at. What you fence off is not merely hidden from the room — it never reaches the part that reads at all. ⚠️ This is also the only moment that works in bulk: letting a whole folder through later is one item at a time, by hand.

9

you point it at your things

A plain folder of notes and pictures, an Obsidian vault, or an export from ChatGPT or Claude. Your own files are never changed — the room keeps its own copies. ⚠️ This is one lump with no resume: close the lid, lose the power or restart part-way, and the whole thing is discarded and begins again.

10

then you wait, and this is the honest part

It takes hours, and nothing on screen tells you which run you got. One real diary library took about eight hours and set nothing aside. Another, with more writing in it, took under five. ⭐ How much you have does not predict it — one run had fewer notes than another and took nearly twice as long, and changing nothing but a folder's name once moved a run by sixty-four times. So: an evening, probably. Possibly two. Nobody can tell you which.

11

the room, the first time

Empty shelf. This is day one and it is meant to look like this — there is nothing to finish here, no streak, no daily goal, no checkmark.

12

it shows you a few things

A few at a time, never everything at once. You say keep, or never show me this again, or not now. Nothing is deleted and nothing nags you.

13

and then you come back

The shelf fills only with what you kept. Your own writing starting to come back to you, a few things at a time — the drip is the point of it, not a shortcoming.

14

you read one back

Opened whole and unedited, exactly as you wrote it. The room quotes; it does not rewrite you.

the rest of the room

Setting it up is the smallest part of it. This is what the room actually does once it is running — and, plainly, which of it you can try today and which is still being built.

the candle — how you ask

you can try this in her room

The candle is the whole of asking. You tap it when you feel like it and it looks through what you have brought in. ⭐ It asks first, every time — it never begins on its own, and it never asks you for anything. In her room the candle works: what comes back is writing the room really made about the day you are standing in.

the librarian, and changing it

not in the demo room

Who does the reading is yours to set, and you can see and change it. Which model writes your reflections, whether it reads closely or quickly, and a plain log of every job it has ever run — clearable, and nothing else goes away with it. ⚠️ None of this is reachable in the demo room, on purpose: there is no key behind that page and nothing there can be made to think or to spend.

photographs

not in the demo room — still being built

Pictures come back too, and the room can say something about one. ⚠️ This is the least finished part and the slowest, and the honest claim is that writing leads and pictures are much further behind. ⛔ There is not a single photograph in the demo room — every one of the things in it is writing — so this is one you cannot try yet anywhere.

keeping a photograph

still being built

When a picture lands hard there is more than one thing you can say back to it, and you can name a person or a pet you would rather not be shown. ⚠️ Designed and decided; not something a stranger can walk into yet.

the blessings notebook

partly in her room

What you keep is written down — a plain notebook of the things you said yes to, so the shelf is not the only record of it. In her room the shelf fills as you keep things; ⚠️ the notebook itself is thinner than it will be, and it is one of the parts still being worked on.

what it costs you

money

Nothing, on a first run. With no key of your own, every part of it happens on your own machine. ⚠️ If you already have a paid key sitting in your shell, it will be used without asking.

hours

The real price. See the waiting step above — an evening is the honest expectation and it is not a promise.

what leaves

Nothing. Not on this path.

what you can do today

You cannot run this yet. But there is a finished room standing already, with a hundred years of Katherine Mansfield's days in it — you can press a date, stand in it, and watch the room hold only what she had written by then.
